 What size do you need?
 What size power station do I need for an electric smoker?
 Look for at least 1,000 W of continuous AC output and 1,000 W of surge. For capacity, an electric smoker averages about 1,000 W, so 8 hours needs roughly 10,000 Wh of rated capacity and 24 hours roughly 30,000 Wh, assuming 80% of rated capacity reaches the outlets.
 How long will a 1,000 Wh power station run an electric smoker?
 About 0.8 h for a generic 1,000 Wh unit, if its inverter can handle the 1,000 W startup surge: roughly 800 Wh (80% of rated) reaches the outlets, divided by an average draw of 1,000 W. Measured models of this size vary; see the table above.

 None of the 34 current models we track runs an electric smoker for 24 hours on one charge. Plan to recharge (solar or grid) during the day, or add an expansion battery.

 A pellet grill is an easy load with one difficult moment. For the first few minutes the hot rod igniter draws a burst — commonly in the 200-500W band, with some larger grills published higher — and then the grill drops to a fan, an auger motor and a controller, which together usually sit somewhere in the 40-60W band for the rest of the cook. That shape is unusual: it means the specification that decides your purchase is the surge rating , not the capacity, and a small unit with a big inverter beats a big unit with a small one. 
 Those are nameplate bands, not a figure for your grill. Read the plate — on a pellet grill it is usually on the back of the hopper or underneath the controller, and it will state the amps or watts the grill draws. Multiply amps by 120 to get watts. Every calculation on this page uses your number, not ours. 
 What a cook actually costs, in watt-hours
 A six-hour cook, worked through
 Ignition: 350W for 5 minutes = 350 x (5 / 60) = 29Wh 
 Startup fan cycle: 150W for 10 minutes = 25Wh 
 Steady running: 50W for 5 hours 45 minutes = 288Wh 
 Total for the cook = 29 + 25 + 288 = about 342Wh 
 On a 288Wh battery: short by roughly an hour 
 On a 1,024Wh battery: the cook uses a third of it 
 Ignition is under 10% of the energy and 100% of the difficulty. The steady draw is what empties the battery, and it is small enough that capacity stops mattering well before the cook ends. 
 Substitute your own plate figure and your own cook length into those four lines. If the total comes out above about 80% of a unit's rated capacity, step up a size — the last 20% of any lithium battery is the part you should not be planning around.

 Three mistakes that cost people a cook
 Sizing on capacity instead of surge. A 2,000Wh unit with a 1,000W inverter can fail to light a grill that a 288Wh unit with a 1,500W surge lights without noticing. Check the surge figure first, always. 
 Forgetting the startup fan cycle. Most pellet grills run the fan hard for several minutes after ignition to establish the fire. That is a second, smaller spike, and a unit that is marginal on the igniter will often trip here instead. 
 Using a long, thin extension cord. Voltage drop across a cheap 16-gauge cord at the end of a 50 ft run is a real effect, and it makes the igniter draw more current for longer. Keep the unit near the grill and use the shortest 12- or 14-gauge cord that reaches. 
 Pellet grills at a tailgate, specifically
 This is the single best argument for a battery over a generator in a stadium lot. A lot of venues restrict or ban fuel generators outright, and the ones that allow them put them a long way from the tailgate. A power station has no exhaust, makes no noise and sits under the table — best generator for tailgating covers the rules problem in detail, and how to power a tailgate adds up a whole setup rather than just the grill. 
 One thing to rule out before you shop: a flat-top electric griddle is not a pellet grill and the arithmetic is nothing alike. A griddle is a 1,500W heating element with no duty cycle, and it will empty any unit on this page in well under an hour. If a griddle is on your list, read what size power station to run an air fryer — it is the same problem with a different box. 
 Running one on solar
 A pellet grill is one of the few cooking loads a panel can genuinely keep up with, because the steady draw is smaller than a single panel's output in reasonable sun. A 200W panel in good conditions outpaces a 50W grill draw with room to spare, which in practice means an indefinite cook. How much solar input do you need covers the realistic-harvest arithmetic, and best portable solar panels for power stations has the panel picks. 
 Pellet stoves are a different question
 Google suggests 'power station for pellet stove' alongside the grill query, and the numbers are not the same. A pellet stove runs a combustion blower, a convection blower and an auger continuously, commonly in the 100-300W band rather than 40-60W, and it runs for days rather than hours. Treat it as a home-backup sizing problem: start at what size power station for a power outage .

 Questions
 Frequently asked questions
 What size power station do I need for a pellet grill? + Pick on surge rating first: you need an inverter that clears your grill's igniter draw, which is commonly in the 200-500W band. For capacity, a 288Wh unit covers roughly five hours of cooking after ignition and a 1,024Wh unit covers a full overnight cook, assuming a 40-60W steady draw. 
 Will a 300W power station run a pellet grill? + Often not, and the reason is the igniter rather than the running load. A 300W continuous inverter with a 600W surge is marginal against a grill whose igniter draws 350-500W for several minutes. A 288Wh unit with a 600W continuous rating and a 1,500W surge is the smaller-but-stronger option. 
 How long will a power station run a pellet grill? + Divide 80% of the battery's watt-hours by your grill's steady draw after ignition. At 50W that is about five hours from 288Wh and about sixteen hours from 1,024Wh. Ignition itself costs under 30Wh, so it barely enters the calculation. 
 Can you run a Traeger or Pit Boss on a battery? + Yes, and it is a common off-grid setup, but check the plate on your specific model rather than the brand. Pellet grills across all brands follow the same shape — a big igniter burst, then a small continuous draw — so the surge rating of the power station is what decides it. 
 Can I run a pellet grill and a slow cooker from one power station? + On a 1,024Wh unit with a 2,000W inverter, yes. A slow cooker is a 200-300W band load, which added to a grill's 50W is inside the output of any mid-size unit; the constraint becomes capacity and outlet count rather than output. Two AC outlets gets used up fast. 
 Is a power station or a generator better for a pellet grill? + A battery, in almost every case. The load is small and continuous, which is what batteries are good at, and the places people smoke off-grid — stadium lots, campgrounds, a driveway at 6am — are the places a fuel generator is restricted, loud or both.

Tailgating is a sacred ritual—the grill, the game, the camaraderie. But if you’re running a pellet smoker, you’ve faced the chronic buzzkill: running out of power mid-brisket. A standard gas generator is noisy, stinks up your spot with fumes, and feels like overkill for a 300W auger and fan. That’s why more tailgaters are switching to battery-based power stations. The question is, which one can actually keep your smoker humming through doubleheaders and overtime?

After a decade of field-testing portable power—from Arizona job sites to off-grid campsites—I’ve learned that not all “portable” stations handle the sustained draw of a pellet smoker. In 2025, the market is flooded with options, but only a few deliver the real-world watt-hours and ruggedness you need for a day-long cook in a dusty parking lot.

This guide breaks down exactly what to look for: how to match watt-hours to your smoker’s appetite, why weather resistance matters more than you think, and why a $20 spare charger can save your whole party. I’ll also walk you through five top contenders—from the high-capacity EF ECOFLOW DELTA 2 to the budget-friendly Anker 535—so you can find the best portable power station for running a pellet smoker at a tailgate party without wasting money on hype.

Why You Need the Best Portable Power Station for Running a Pellet Smoker at a Tailgate Party

I've lost count of how many tailgates I've seen ruined by a generator. The noise drowns out pregame banter, the exhaust blows smoke into someone's face, and the constant refueling is a hassle nobody needs when they're trying to nail a pork shoulder. A pellet smoker only pulls about 250-400 watts during operation—just enough to run the auger, fan, and controller. That's well within the range of modern battery power stations.

The real question isn't whether a power station can run your smoker. It's whether it can run it long enough. Most tailgate parties run 6-8 hours, and your smoker will cycle on and off as it maintains temperature. In my testing, a 300W smoker running at a 50% duty cycle consumes about 150W per hour. That means you need at least 900Wh of usable capacity for a full day of cooking. If you're also running a fridge for drinks or meats, check out our guide on the best portable power station for running a 12v refrigerator for 24 hours off grid for more capacity planning tips.

The EF ECOFLOW Portable Power Station DELTA 2 sits at the top of my recommendation list here. With 1024Wh of LiFePO₄ battery capacity and 1800W AC output, it's the only station I trust for all-day cooks without babysitting the battery gauge. Meanwhile, the Goal Zero Yeti Portable Power Station, Yeti 300 offers a different trade-off. At 297Wh, it won't run a smoker all day, but its weather-sealed design makes it the best option for tailgaters who prioritize durability over runtime—especially in unpredictable weather.

Understanding watt-hours versus running watts will save you from buying a station that dies at halftime. Here's the simple formula I use: take your smoker's rated wattage, multiply by the percentage of time it actually runs (usually 40-60%), and that's your hourly consumption. Divide your power station's watt-hours by that number, and you get estimated runtime.

For a typical 300W pellet smoker running 50% duty cycle: 150W per hour. A 512Wh station gives you about 3.4 hours of run time. A 1024Wh station gives you nearly 7 hours.

The Anker 535 Portable Power Station with Carrying Case Bag hits a sweet spot for budget-conscious tailgaters with smaller smokers. Its 512Wh capacity and 500W inverter can handle a 4-6 hour cook if you're running a smaller unit or supplement with a cooler. The included carrying case is a nice bonus for protecting your investment in a crowded parking lot.

If you're running a larger smoker or planning for overtime, the EF ECOFLOW Portable Power Station DELTA 2 is the clear winner. Its 1024Wh capacity means you can start smoking at 8 AM and still have 30% battery left when the game ends at 4 PM. No mid-game power anxiety. Frequently Asked Questions
Can I run a pellet smoker off a portable power station all day?

Yes, but you need a unit with at least 1,000Wh capacity. A pellet smoker typically draws 150-300 watts during startup and 50-80 watts while cooking. For a full tailgate party (6-8 hours), look for a portable power station with 1,200Wh or more to avoid running out of power.

What size inverter do I need for a pellet smoker at a tailgate?

You need a pure sine wave inverter rated for at least 500 watts continuous. Most pellet smokers require 300 watts to ignite the auger and fan, but a 500W inverter provides a safe buffer. Avoid modified sine wave inverters, as they can damage the smoker's control board.

How do I keep my pellet smoker running during a long tailgate?

Pair your portable power station with a 100-watt solar panel for top-off charging during the day. Start with a full charge and run the smoker on the "smoke" or low setting to conserve battery. Avoid opening the lid frequently, as this triggers the auger to burn more power.

Should I get a lithium or lead-acid power station for a pellet smoker?

Lithium (LiFePO4) is far better for tailgate parties. It is lighter to carry, provides more usable capacity (up to 90%), and lasts 3,000+ charge cycles versus 500 for lead-acid. For running a pellet smoker, lithium handles the constant power draw more efficiently.

When should I recharge my power station while smoking meat?

Recharge when the battery drops to 30-40% capacity, not when it's nearly dead. Most portable power stations have a battery percentage display. If you are smoking for over 6 hours, plug into a car outlet (if your unit supports 12V charging) during lunch to extend runtime.

Conclusion: Powering the Tailgate, Not Complicating It

After twelve years in this field—from testing LiFePO₄ cells in Arizona heat to troubleshooting inverters on remote job sites—I’ve learned that the best portable power station for a pellet smoker isn’t the one with the flashiest display or the highest peak wattage. It’s the one that delivers clean, sustained power for the duration of your cook, without tripping on start-up surges or leaving you stranded mid-afternoon. For a typical tailgate, a unit with at least 700Wh capacity and a pure sine wave inverter rated for 1,200W continuous will handle most smokers comfortably. Look for low-temperature cutoffs and true pass-through charging if you’re running from a vehicle battery. As of 2025, the market has matured dramatically, but marketing still outpaces physics—your smoker’s controller doesn’t care about brand hype, only voltage stability.

The information provided here reflects my engineering experience and field testing, not professional legal or medical advice. Always verify your specific smoker’s start-up load and local tailgate regulations before purchasing.

Take the specs from your smoker’s manual, calculate the runtime you need, and cross-reference with a unit’s continuous output (not surge). If you want a sure bet, start with a reputable 1,000Wh LiFePO₄ station and test it at home before game day. You’ve got the gear—now go enjoy the cook.

 Reliable power is the foundation of any legendary BBQ. Whether you’re chasing the "stall" during a 12-hour backyard brisket session, tailgating at the stadium, or fighting for a podium finish in a pro competition, a sudden power interruption is the enemy. It doesn’t just stop the clock; it risks the "blue smoke" quality and can turn a $150 Prime Grade brisket into a very expensive piece of shoe leather.
 While old-school gas generators were once the only choice for off-grid power, they are loud, vibrate, and kick out exhaust that nobody wants near their food. A BLUETTI portable power station is a cleaner, silent alternative that is safe to run in "indoor-adjacent" spaces like an open garage or under a pop-up tent. It acts as an insurance policy for your meat, ensuring your low-and-slow automated systems stay humming until that bark is set to perfection.
 Pellet Grill Power Consumption: The Real Numbers
 Wood pellets provide the thermal mass and heat, but electricity runs the "brains" and the mechanical guts of your pit. If the power drops, the auger stops, and your bark is history.
 How Pellet Grills Actually Work
 Electricity drives three core components that maintain your cooking environment:
 The Auger Motor: A motorized screw that feeds pellets into the fire pot. If this stops, your fire dies.
 The Combustion Fan: This blower provides oxygen to the fire and creates the convection needed for even cooking.
 The Digital Controller: This manages the PID algorithms and Wi-Fi connections. It’s the most sensitive part of your rig.
 Wattage by Operation Mode
 Power draw isn't a flat line; it spikes and dips based on the phase of the cook:
 Startup/Ignition: This is the danger zone. The igniter rod (hot rod) draws 250–600W for the first 5–10 minutes to light the fire. You need a power station that can handle this initial surge without tripping.
 Steady Cooking: Once the fire is roaring, the igniter shuts off. Low-temp smoking (180–225°F) typically pulls a modest 50–100W. High-heat searing (400–500°F) forces the fan and auger into higher duty cycles, drawing 200–400W.

 Power Station FAQs 
 A power station (also called a portable power station, battery generator, or Solar generator) is a rechargeable battery-powered device that supplies electricity to your devices and appliances, like phones, laptops, CPAP machines, refrigerators, and more. It provides quiet, fume-free power for essential home backup, camping and outdoor adventures, worksites, DIY projects, and more. 
 Our product selector helps you easily compare power stations of different sizes based on what you want to power. Note: The estimated runtime is for each individual item when powered independently, starting with a full charge. Powering multiple items will reduce the runtimes shown due to increased power consumption. 
 While both power stations and generators can provide electricity during an outage or off-grid use, they work very differently. 
 A power station is a battery-powered device that stores energy and delivers it silently through built-in outlets and USB ports. It produces no emissions, requires very little maintenance, and is safe to use indoors, making it ideal for apartments, RVs, tents, and limited home backup during storms. You can recharge it from a wall outlet, solar panels, or even a car charger. 
 On the other hand, generators run on fuel like gasoline, propane or natural gas. They generate electricity from an internal combustion engine, which makes it noisy, produces fumes, and requires outdoor use only for safety. Generators usually provide more raw power and can run indefinitely as long as you keep refueling, but they require more upkeep maintenance than a power station. 
 Charge cycle life refers to how many full charge-and-discharge cycles a battery can go through before its capacity begins to noticeably decline. Over time, every battery slowly loses its ability to hold a full charge, but how fast that happens depends on the battery chemistry used. 
 Predator power stations use LFP ( LiFePO 4 ‐Lithium Iron Phosphate ) battery cells, which offer exceptional durability. LFP batteries typically maintain 80% or more of their original capacity after 3500+ full charge cycles . That means even if you use and recharge your power station every single day , it can last for 10 years or more with proper care. 
 Predator power stations can be charged using: 
 A standard wall outlet (AC)
 Solar panels (optional add-on). All Predator power stations come with built-in MPPT solar charge controllers and solar charging cables.

 Connecting a solar panel to a power station is usually straightforward, but there are a few important things to keep in mind to ensure safe and efficient charging. 
 First, check your power station's maximum solar input voltage and current. This information is typically listed on the product label and in the user manual. Then, compare that to your solar panel's output voltage and current to make sure they're compatible. If you're using more than one solar panel, you'll need to decide whether to connect them in series (which increases voltage) or parallel (which increases current). Choosing the right configuration depends on your power station's input limits. Please note that exceeding the voltage limit can trigger a safety shutoff or even damage the unit.
